1 Introduction
Open innovation describes the opening of innovation processes in order to involve external stakeholders such
as customers, experts and partner organisations in the development of new products, services or technologies.
Digital platforms play a decisive role here by overcoming geographical and organisational boundaries, and enabling
the exchange of knowledge in global networks. Digital open innovation platforms use digital technologies to
promote collaborative processes. They make it easier for companies and projects to develop innovative ideas,
collect data and implement solutions. The effectiveness of such platforms has been proven by various studies.
For example, one study showed that 64-77% of companies that use open innovation approaches profit from a
combination of internal and external stimuli to successfully implement their innovative projects. Companies
that combine external and internal sources of knowledge increase the success rate of new products by up to 19%
compared to purely internal approaches. Another example of the efficiency of digital open innovation platforms is
Kaggle, a platform that organises data science competitions. Studies show that a high level of engagement can be
achieved through competition formats and targeted incentives. Crowd-funding platforms such as Kickstarter
are similarly successful, with projects that interact with their target group at an early stage achieving up to 65%
higher success rates. This illustrates the importance of interaction and transparency in the innovation process.
Despite these successes, digital platforms face specific challenges. The protection of intellectual property, longterm
user loyalty and the continuous further development of technological standards are decisive factors. Statistics
show that up to 50% of newly founded platforms fail within the first five years, often due to a lack of user loyalty
or ineffective monetisation strategies. In the wind energy industry, it is well known that a lack of data and
knowledge sharing is an issue. The lack of data maturity in the sector results in inefficiencies in handling
and creating insights from the large volume of data produced throughout the lifecycle of a wind energy project.
For example, operational data formats are not consistent across different software solutions used to monitor and
operate wind farms, and key metadata are often lacking. The goal of the work presented here is to assess the overall
feasibility of a digital open innovation platform for the wind energy sector, based on a concrete case study.
title: Assessing the feasibility of a digital open innovation platform for the wind energy sector
